  Regular Meeting Minutes
  February 12, 2025

CALL TO ORDER - Chair Flores called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.

FLAG SALUTE - by Secretary Pelayo

Chair Flores called for a moment of silence for the passing of former Police Chief Robert Todd.

ROLL CALL - by Ana Medina, Executive Assistant
Present: Chair Flores, Vice Chair Lizette Ruiz, Secretary Edgar Pelayo and Commissioner Cynthia Esquivel.
Commissioner Alejanda Flores had an excused absence.
Staff: Director of Parks & Recreation Steve Costley, Deputy Director Tina Fierro, and Parks Superintendent
Glenn Massey.

APPROVAL OF MEETING MINUTES FOR DECEMBER 12, 2024
Recommended Motion: Motion to approve the minutes as presented.
M/S/C: Vice Chair Ruiz/Secretary Pelayo to approve the minutes as presented.
PUBLIC COMMENTS
Recognized: Mario Dominguez requested the splash pad issue be on a future meeting.
Recognized: Angeline, stated the traveling team Poison went from three games a month to only one,
please look into what can be done.
Recognized: Sofia said she enjoys being on the team but doesn’t like playing only once a month.

PRESENTATION - None

OPEN SESSION ITEMS

1. ELECTION OF OFFICERS/REORGANIZATION
Recommended Motion: Motion for Commission to nominate and approve a Chair, Vice Chair, and
Secretary for the coming year.
M/S/C: Vice Chair Ruiz/Secretary Pelayo to keep the board as is with Commissioner Esquivel as Secretary.
Director Costley reviewed this item; a discussion ensued.

2. RECREATION PROGRAMING REPORT 2ND QUARTER FY 2024/25
Recommended Motion: Motion to receive and file.
M/S/C: Secretary Pelayo/Commissioner Esquivel
Deputy Director Fierro reviewed this item; a discussion ensued.
Director Costley complemented the Commission as being most active in Park events.
Vice Chair Ruiz asked if the cost of light at Hollydale Regional Park was shared with AYSO, replied no, the
City foots the bill.

3. GROUNDS & PARKS FACILITY MAINTENANCE REPORT 2ND QUARTER FY 2024/25
Recommended Motion: Motion to receive and file.
M/S/C: Vice Chair Ruiz/Secretary Pelayo
Parks Supt. Massey reviewed this item; a discussion ensued.

  4
 Parks Supt. Massey stated staff has renovated the horseshoe pits and explained what that entails. They
also renovated Diamond 5 & 8. Irrigation repair and maintenance is ongoing. Small trees have been raised
at the west side parks to ease mowing. Staff replaced 10 drinking fountains in South Gate Park. There were
broken main and lateral irrigation lines in Hollydale Regional Park that staff repaired. Staff installed two
new sand bunkers in the Golf Course, also the greens were aerified. A discussion ensued.

DIRECTOR'S REPORT / CALENDAR OF EVENTS
Director Costley: The Hollydale Community Park reopening was very successful. Circle Parks is still in
progress. Pickle Ball courts have been installed in SG Park’s Tennis Court. Orban Orchard is moving
quickly, with a possible June opening. Due to budget constraints the new Parks Master Plan had to be
cancelled.

Deputy Dir. Fierro: Mentioned upcoming special events. Trips have been very strong. The Annual Sports
Center Open House was a huge success. The new event Ties & Tiaras was a great event, very good
comments. Tonight, a full bus went to the UCLA vs USC Women’s basketball game at the Galen Center.
Golf tournament this Sunday. Both full time and hourly staff are working hard to bring the best events
possible. The quarterly brochure has gone to print and will come out soon.
Easter Fest, April 12; Easter Splash, April 13; Youth Sports Camp, April 14-18, ages 7-12; Mom Prom, April
26; Art Exhibit Opening Playgrounds/Jugamos, May 3; to name a few

Parks Supt. Massey: Tree trimming at Hollydale Regional Park is ongoing. Ball field renovations is also
ongoing. Staff began soccer field renovation at Hollydale Regional Park.

PARKS & RECREATION COMMISSION SUB-COMMITTEE REPORTS
Vice Chair Ruiz: Was impressed with the turnout at the Hollydale Community Park reopening.

Secretary Pelayo: No comment

Commissioner Flores: No comment

REQUEST FOR ITEMS ON FUTURE AGENDAS
Secretary Pelayo would like to have a report on the public’s response of the survey and a discussion of the
splash pad. A report on revenue generating opportunities. Deputy Dir. Fierro stated the survey would
remain open until the end of summer, a report would probably be brought in September.
Vice Chair Ruiz would like a report on why the traveling team was cut to only once a month.
Commissioner Esquivel wanted the status of the shade for Diamonds 8 & 10.

ADJOURNMENT - At 8:15 p.m. Chair Flores asked for a motion to adjourn.
M/S/C: Commissioner Esquivel/Vice Chair Ruiz

Respectfully submitted:

Edgar Pelayo, Secretary

Subject:  HSA Annual  Report  for 2024

Recommended  Motion:  Motion to Receive  and File

Report Summary:  Since 2006, the Human Services Association  (HSA) has operated
the City's two Community  Resource Center buildings; the Westside Center on State
Street and the Hollydale Center on Industrial Avenue.  As part of their operating
agreements,  HSA is required to submit a report to the Commission annually indicating
their activities and accomplishments  over the past year. The report for 2024 is attached
for the Commission's  review.

The purpose of these agreements  is to take facilities that the City may not be able to
afford to operate and make them useful to the Community while supporting a local non-
profit organization.  As is demonstrated,  HSA provides a wide variety of Social and
Community Services from these facilities, primarily to South Gate residents.  By utilizing
these facilities in this way and creating partnerships,  the City is able to provide a wider
variety of service and therefore meet many community needs that might not otherwise be
met.

In addition to the programs that HSA would normally run, our agreement requires them
to offer afterschool tutoring during the school year. HSA is also required by the terms of
the agreement to have a Neighborhood  Advisory Committee to recommend additional
programs that would benefit the surrounding community.

Along with City staff, a representative  from HSA will be present to answer any questions.

The most  important  goal of our early  childhood  curriculum  is to help children  become  enthusiastic
learners.  This means  encouraging  children  to be active  and creative  explorers  who  are not afraid
to  try  out  their  ideas  and  to  think  their  own  thoughts.  Our  goal  is to help  children  become
independent,  self-confident,  inquisitive  learners.  We are teaching  them  how  to learn,  not just  in
preschool,  but all through  their  lives.  We are allowing  them  to learn  at their  own pace and in the
ways  that are best for them.  We are giving  those  good  habits  and attitudes,  particularly  a positive
sense of themselves,  which  will  make  a difference  throughout  their  lives.

The  activities  we  plan  for  children,  the  way  we  organize  the  environment,  select  toys  and

HSA  Pasitos  Early  Childhood  Education  Department  utilizes  the High/Scope  Curriculum.  The
selected  curriculum  ensure  alignment  witli  the  California  Preschool  Learning  Foundations  and
California  Preschool  Curriculum  Framework,  School  Readiness  Goals,  Ongoing  Assessment
(DRDP  2015),  and the integration  of service  areas into the curriculum.

The  High/Scope  Curriculum  emphasizes  on "active  participatory  learning".  High/Scope  is a
comprehensive  educational  approach  that strives  to help children  to develop  in all areas.

High/Scope  focuses  on the following  fundamental  principles:
  I  To learn through  active  involvement  with  people,  materials,  events  and ideas.
  I  To become  independent,  responsible  and confident  - ready  for school  and ready  for life.
  I  To learn  to plan  many  of their  own  activities,  carry  them  out and talk  with  others  about
  what they have done and what  they have planned.

In the classrooms,  the teachers  follow  a predictable  sequence  of events known  as the daily  routine.
This provides  a structure  within  the children  to make  choices  and decisions,  follow  their  interests,
and develop  tlieir  abilities  in each content  area.

The  outdoor  environment  is reflective  of the  classroom  environment.  Within  this  structure,
teachers  organize  child-initiated  and teacher-directed  learning  experiences  that  are intended  to
address  the developmental  areas of learning.  Through  experiences  with  materials  in the different
sites, verbal  interactions  with  peers,  and scaffold  instruction  with  adults,  the child  is expected  to
learn  and develop  in all  areas.  The  goal  is for  children  to become  independent,  self-confident,
inquisitive  and enthusiastic  learners  to acquire  school  readiness  skills  necessary  for the future.

Family  Advocates  are  committed  to  supporting  parents  as they  navigate  the  transition  to

Early  Head Start at the Hollydale  Center

a variety  of  experiences  for  the  development  of  the  child's  fullest  potential  are provided
through  this  program,  which  has  a strong  commitment  to the  community.  This  involvement
has been at the core of the development  of many  social  service  programs  offered  through  HSA.  A
variety  of experiences  for the development  of the child's  fullest  potential  are provided  through  this

The  High  Scope  Curriculum  emphasizes  on "Active  Participatory  Learning."  High  Scope  is a
comprehensive  educational  approach  that strives  to help  children  to develop  in all areas. In the
classrooms,  the teachers  follow  a predictable  sequence  of events  known  as the daily  routine.  This
provides  a structure  within  the children  to make  choices  and decisions,  follow  their  interest,  and
develop  their  abilities  in each content  area.

In the 2024-25  academic  year,  we embarked  on tlie  third  year  of implementing  the Conscious
Discipline  curriculum,  aimed  at supporting  teachers  in managing  behavioral  issues within  their
classrooms.  Conscious  Discipline  is  an  evidence-based,  trauma-informed  approach.  It
is recognized  by the Substance  Abuse  and Mental  Health  Administration's  (SAMHSA's)  National
Registry  of Evidence-based  Programs  and Practices  (NREPP),  and received  high ratings  in 8 of 10
categories  in a Harvard  analysis  of the nation's  top 25 social-emotional  learning  programs.  The
Harvard study's authors say,"Conscious Discipline provides an array of behavior management
strategies  and classroom  structures  that teachers  can use to turn everyday  situations  irtto learning
opportunities  "

The core methodology  is based on four  essential  components  that are scientifically  and practically
design  for success:

  J  Brain  State  Model:  The Conscious  Discipline  Brain  State Model  recognizes  three basic
  brain  / body  / mind  states likely  to produce  certain  behaviors.  Intentional,  state-  specific
  responses  enable  access to advanced  skills.
  I  Seven  Powers  for  Conscious  Adults:  The  seven  powers  create  a shift  in the way  adults
  see conflict  so we can maintain  composure  and consciously  respond  to difficult  situations.
  Adults'  ability  to self-regulate  is the precursor  to teaching  children  social-emotional  skills.
  J  Creating  the  School  Family:  The  School  Family  increases  connections  between  adults
  and children  at all levels,  ensuring  optimal  development  for all. A School  Family  culture
  is built  tlirough  consistent  modeling  of routines,  rituals  and structures.
  I  Seven  Skills  of Discipline:  These  seven  skills  transform  everyday  discipline  issues  into
  teachable  moments,  equipping  children  with  the  social-emotional  and  communication
  skills  needed  to manage  themselves  resolve  conflict  and develop  healthy  behavior.

Throughout  the academic  year,  our program  prioritized  mental  health  support  for staff,  children,
and families.  To address  the growing  need in this area, we expanded  our team by hiring  additional
staff  to provide  mental  health  services  and  support  for  special  education.  This  decision  was
prompted  by an increase  in children  exhibiting  areas of concern  in these domains,  as well  as a rise
in the number  of children  with  special  needs.

Fuithermore,  workforce  shortages  have posed  a challenge  for our program,  as we actively  sought
qualified  teachers  capable  of offering  care to both  children  and families  within  our program  and
the wider  community.

list for children  seeking  admission.  This  shortage  is particularly  pronounced  for programs  catering
to children  below  the age of three.

Report Summary:

Special Events:
Summer Concerts in the Park Series were held every Friday night in July at the South
Gate Bandstand. The series included the following bands: Corazon de Mana, Los Del
Momento, Grupo Neblina, and Mariachi Divas. Our new and improved concert series
featured the TAP truck beer garden, food trucks, vendors, youth/adult sports staff
leading Rec on the Run, and our Cultural Arts staff leading art activities every week.
Each week the beer garden included cocktail tables, color changing cups (with Concert
logo), and board games. Three to four different food trucks were available each week
for all concert goers to enjoy a bite to eat while listening to the performances. Tampico
& Celsius were in attendance every week with giveaways galore. Rec on the Run
included jumbo sized yard games, pick up soccer games, cornhole tournaments, and
more. The art activities offered included: DIY band patches, conga drums, and
sombreros. This concert series provided opportunities for all ages to be entertained and
enjoy a nice relaxing summer evening at the park. Due to the newly added
improvements, we’ve seen a significant increase in attendance and averaged between
600-700 attendees.

Summer Movies in the Park Series was held every Friday night in August at the South
Gate Golf Course. The series included the following movies: Kung Fu Panda 4,
Haunted Mansion, Trolls - Band Together, Wonka, and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
Mutant Mayhem. This summer series also had a new addition of a snack/ice cream
truck being in site for each movie. The snack/ ice cream truck was well received and
remained consistently busy the entirety of the movie. Each movie night averaged
approximately 200 attendees.

Our first ever Family Night was held, and it was Game Night edition - Minute to Win It.
This event had 40 registered participants and families battled it out at the Girls Club
House. The event featured various 1-minute challenges from the game show “Minute to
Win It”. Families were shown a preview clip of the challenge and would then decide

  Page 1 of 6  19
 who from their team would compete. This event catered to all ages and anyone could
participate, we had 5-year-olds competing against seniors. Once the competition was
over, families enjoyed a nice dinner that consisted of pizza, salad, and dessert. The
overall winning team received free admission to our next Family Night (Reptile Show)
on November 15.

On October 31, at South Gate Park our team hosted our Annual Halloween Haunt
event. This year we had a complete re-vamp and setup that featured our Show Mobile
as the main stage. At the main stage we hosted our costume contest, stage games and
ended the evening with a dance contest full of great energy. The event also included
Halloween decorations throughout, DIY slime kits, DIY cookie decorating kits,
photobooths, game booths, jumpers, trackless trains, and food trucks. The event was
heavily promoted through marquees, billboards, our brochure, and social media outlets
which ensured a great turnout.

Our 2nd Family Night in November was our sold-out Reptile Show, we had 50 registered
attendees. Paramount Pet Entertainment hosted a 2-hour interactive reptile show that
allowed participants to end the evening holding a 15-foot python. The event also
included arts and crafts, and a family dinner.

The Veteran’s Day event was held on November 9, and we had approximately 50
attendees. This year’s guest speaker was FC1 (SW) Felicia Dawn Luna who is also a
South Gate resident. Felicia was presented with a proclamation and recognized for her
service. Kiwani’s Kids were also a part of the program as they prepared and read their
“Thank you” Veteran letters. Light refreshments and beverages were available for all in
attendance. After the completion of Veteran’s Day, staff headed over to table a booth at
Family Day in the Park. Our information booth promoted upcoming events and a
plethora of giveaways.

Santa’s Breakfast was held on Saturday, December 9 and had 400 registered
attendees. The event included a delicious breakfast, a “new” hot chocolate station,
holiday crafts, raffle prizes, and photos with Santa. Each child was able to walk away
with a special gift from Santa. Volunteers from the Key Club and Miss South Gate
assisted in making the event a success.

Our first ever Tiaras and Ties Dance was held in January at the Girls Club House. This
sold-out event celebrated the special bond between father (or special male figure) and
daughters. All attendees enjoyed a magical evening from 6:00pm to 8:00pm. Guests
arrived in formal attire and were treated to a lively DJ, a photo booth, and a delicious
dinner featuring chicken fettuccine alfredo, side salad, dessert, and drinks. The evening
included line dances, a traditional father-daughter dance, and the Stroll. The venue was
beautifully decorated, creating an enchanting atmosphere. Each girl and her male guest
received a special gift to commemorate the night, making it a truly unforgettable
experience.

For Easter Fest 2025, our team prepared a fun-filled day full of activities at the South
Gate Golf Course. Eggs, bags, wristbands, and snow cone supplies have been
purchased. Carnival games and our bunny photo area supplies are also ready. DJ
Gilbert, a photo booth, two face painters, a food truck, and a soft play area have also

  Page 2 of 6  20
 been secured to enhance the event overall. Our goal this year was to create lasting
memories for all ages; we have activities planned for everyone to participate in. Anyone
from the age of 6 months old in the soft play area to our seniors who can participate in
our first ever adult egg hunt. The event is sold out and set to take place next quarter.

Mom Prom was new this year and held in the month of April at the Girls Club House.
This event was also sold-out and provided the opportunity for Mothers (or special
female figures) and their sons to enjoy an evening full of fun. Guests arrived in their 80’s
retro themed attire and were treated to a lively DJ, a photo booth, and a delicious dinner
featuring chicken fettuccine alfredo, side salad, dessert, and drinks. The venue was
beautifully decorated, and the black lights really made the neon décor pop. Each boy
and his female guest received a special gift to end the evening.

Youth Programs:
Tiny Two’s and Tot Time class offerings fluctuated quarterly due to staff shortages.
Participants of summer enjoyed classroom time with endless summer themed projects
and excursions for all participants to enjoy. Thankfully the wonderful California weather
was in our favor and our team made a visit to Wild Rivers. Tot Time and Tiny Two’s
concluded their summer sessions with the GCH Main Hall being transformed into
toddler heaven with a worm play pen, slide, small jumper, mini basketball court and
tricycles. In addition to the play area our classes collaborated with the pool and
provided an end of session pool party for classes.

New for the Fall session, staff organized a Trunk or Treat event that was held on
October 29 and 30 for all Tiny Two and Tot Time program participants. We had over 50
decorated vehicles and participating families across both days. Families really got into
the Halloween spirit and proudly decorated their themed trunks for the children to enjoy.
All participating vehicles were recognized and received a Halloween themed certificate,
and our 3 winners were crowned in the following categories: Spookiest, Funniest, and
Most Creative. The event included music, photo areas, a costume parade, and trunk-or-
treating, with candy provided by the organizers and donations.

Spring Session for Tot Time and Tiny 2’s was all about excursions. In addition to the
classroom setting and learning, our participants had the opportunity to attend two
amazing excursions. Our first excursion was to the LA County Fair where our
participants started with a tour of the barn, gardens, and farm animal exhibitions. Once
the fair opened our groups were able to head in and enjoy all the fair offerings. The
second excursion planned was Adventure City, a toddler amusement park. This trip
was well received and hit maximum capacity within a few days. Participants were able
to ride mini roller coasters, trains, and a carousel.

Lil Chefs had 2 class offerings every quarter for this class series, all 8 classes reached
maximum participants on the first day of registration. Our 5-week cooking series taught
children safety, etiquette, and how to prepare dishes like wonton tacos, BBQ chicken
roll ups, Cornish hens, fruit parfaits, and other delicious desserts.

Teen Programs:

 This year Teen programming was frozen due to the vacancy of our Full Time Recreation
Coordinator. We are thrilled that we were able to fill the position in June and are
currently in the beginning phases of a Teen program re-vamp.

Senior Services:
Summer at the senior center introduced exciting options like yoga, Lotería, and a mental
health support group. All new editions were designed to enhance and enrich the lives of
our seniors. Of course, our beloved bingo continues to draw in a large crowd on
Wednesday afternoons, along with lively dance and karaoke sessions on Thursday
mornings. The HSA lunch program remains a cornerstone of our offerings, providing
healthy meals every day. Additionally, we hosted special presentations from various
insurance providers to keep our seniors informed about upcoming changes to Medicare
and medical enrollment. The summers scheduled trips included: Valley View Casino,
Orange County Fair, Soboba Casino, Agua Caliente Casino, The Grove, Newport
Whale Watching Tour, Catalina Island, Festival of Art and ended with a trip to Solvang.

Fall at the Senior Center again presented a new and engaging activity for our seniors.
Our new offering: an ESL class tailored specifically for seniors and a program through
HSA that provided healthy food and easy recipe options for seniors to try at home. The
Senior Center held a variety of exciting events. The Halloween social was a hit with
seniors, featuring raffle prizes, goody bags, and a DJ. In November, Alta Med hosted an
event filled with games and prizes for the seniors, and in December, a local choir
performed for them during lunch. Before our Christmas break, they had their annual
Christmas social, which included the 25 Days of Christmas raffle and treat bags for all.
In addition to these events, we scheduled nine trips for our seniors. These trips included
visits to Fantasy Casino, Getty Villa, Tanaka Farm, Día de Los Muertos celebrations in
Hollywood and San Diego, Morongo Casino, Winter Fest, Vejas Casino, and a holiday
cruise.

Winter season was exceptionally active, with a full calendar of excursions and events
that brought our senior community together in joyful and meaningful ways. In February,
we partnered with Alta Med to host a special Valentine’s Day event for our seniors. Love
and friendship were in the air as this event featured a DJ, a jewelry maker, and
numerous raffles. Continuing our commitment to supporting the emotional well-being of
our seniors, our center has maintained a strong partnership with Los Angeles Mental
Health. The senior support group, launched last year, expanded due to high demand
and now meets three times a week, offering an essential resource for mental health
support. Winter adventures had nine scheduled trips, including visits to Disney on Ice,
Pala Casino, Palm Springs Tram, Harrah’s Casino, the Museum of Neon, Huntington
Library, Pauma Casino, the theatrical performance of Harry Potter & The Cursed Child,
and Descanso Gardens.

Spring season like in years past was no different, we again were a part of the Annual
Southeast Senior Ball, this event originated here in South Gate and has grown
exponentially over the years. This year’s event was hosted between 12 participating
cities at the Commerce Casino. Each city chartered in 50 of their own seniors to enjoy
a catered lunch, coffee bar, photo booth, and giveaways. The dance floor was jam
packed and many memories were made.

 Contract Classes:
Our core group of offerings of baby boogie, folklorico, ballet, hip hop, tap, tumbling,
cheerleading, and self-defense remained steady across this fiscal year. With offerings
varying Monday through Thursday evenings, it was easy for participants to find
something that accommodated their family’s schedule. Registration for these classes
on average reached maximum capacity every quarter with a slight dip in the winter due
to the colder weather. Our amazing contractors and the classes they teach keep our
participants consistently coming back for more.

At the end of each quarter, participants had the option to perform in our dance recitals.
Our dance recitals were held at the end of the nine-week sessions and students were
able to showcase their new skills and dance routines. All recitals were held in the Henry
C. Gonzalez Auditorium and spanned over three nights with an average audience of
350-500 each night. Our participants and their families really enjoyed these recitals as
they are the culmination of their child’s nine weeks of learning.

Golf Course:
This year on the Golf Course, we maintained a lively blend of our regular players while
welcoming many fresh faces. Our course also served as the backdrop for local high
schools’ practices and matches. Guests enjoyed playing nine holes on a meticulously
maintained green, enhanced by a few new changes to the course. We hosted four
exciting quarterly golf tournaments throughout the year that drew in large crowds. Each
tournament winner was awarded a trophy and golf themed prizes.

Cultural Arts:
Summer for our Cultural Arts division began with the hosting of their Third Annual Zine
Fiesta which included curating vendors, mapping out the layout, promotion on social
media, and the distribution of printed mini posters and flyers. The Zine Fiesta was held
in conjunction with the opening of our Oír de Nuevo/Press Repeat exhibit and The
Eastside Exhibition partnership (group art exhibit that highlights local printmakers). New
to our exhibit this quarter was open studio Saturdays and themed drop-in art activities.
Our guitar picks charm bracelets/necklaces were a hit! Additional collaborations the
team was able to participate in was an art activity at the Chicxs Rockerxs SELA 10 th
year anniversary of their end of camp showcase. Arts for LA ACTIVATE program came
to an end and our team was hard at work organizing the final event: Art & Picnic - Picnic
at the Museum! The cohort decided to celebrate in Southeast Los Angeles and the
event was held at our Museum & Art Gallery.

Cultural Arts kicked off fall with hosting their 4th Annual South Gate Art Walk which had
5 workshops led by partner organizations, 2 live DJs, 4 live performances, 2 live visual
artists, 45 vendors/artisans, 2 art exhibits and the museum permanent collection on
display along with SG Sounds and a new section of the museum that displayed historic
kitchenette and tools, and an Amelia Earhart display. Back again this year was the
Community Altar that had 37 photo submissions of community loved ones who have
passed. Our team edited and framed photos and made clay Pan De Muertos to place
onto the altar. The Community Altar was built in the City Hall lobby that was on view for
a week. After our Community Altar, our team worked with the Chicxs Rockerxs SELA
again to curate and exhibit 10 years’ worth of camp rock magic. The opening reception
of the museum exhibit was on Saturday, November 16. There was a full exhibit in the

CRSELA exhibition. NBC 4 Los Angeles highlighted the exhibition in one of their
